The Mountain viscacha rat (Octomys mimax) is a relatively large-bodied octodontid rodent endemic to the rocky slopes of the central Andes. Data from captive colonies curated at standard physiological temperatures of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have been used to estimate several key life-history traits by analogy with better-studied congeners. Maximum longevity in captivity is estimated at approximately six years [am = approximately six years], a figure consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in other octodontids of similar body mass at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Gestation in this species is thought to be prolonged, with comparative data from Octodontomys gliroides suggesting a gestation time of 104 days [tg = 104 days] when females are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended intrauterine development likely reflects the energetic demands of producing a relatively precocial neonate. The ultimate wet weight of the Mountain viscacha rat ranges from 85 to 121 grams [Wwi = 85 to 121 grams], placing it among the larger members of its family. Adult body mass in this species shows minimal sexual dimorphism.

Birth in Octomys mimax, by extrapolation from the closely related red viscacha rat (Tympanoctomys barrerae), is expected to result in a neonate weighing approximately 4 grams [Wwb = approximately 4 grams]. This neonatal mass is modest for an octodontid of its ultimate size, suggesting a strategy of investing in relatively altricial young despite the prolonged gestation. Weaning, the critical transition from milk dependency to nutritional independence, is estimated to occur at 92 days after birth [tx = 92 days after birth] under the thermal conditions typical of maternal care (37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]). This interval allows the growing juvenile to achieve a substantial portion of its adult size before making the dietary shift to the fibrous vegetation that characterizes the adult diet. The time since birth at weaning is an important developmental milestone, marking the cessation of lactation by the female and the onset of independent foraging in the harsh, arid environment the species inhabits.

Reproductive output in the Mountain viscacha rat is inferred from patterns observed in Octodontomys gliroides. A typical litter consists of two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter], and females are thought capable of raising approximately two litters each year [F_R_i = approximately two litters each year] under favorable conditions when maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This reproductive schedule yields a moderate annual reproductive rate, balancing the energetic constraints of lactation and the need to accumulate sufficient body reserves between breeding events. The production of twinning as the standard litter size is consistent with many other octodontid rodents and may reflect an optimization between offspring size and maternal metabolic capacity in a resource-limited environment. Field records suggest that this rate is seldom achieved in the wild during periods of drought.

The onset of puberty in Octomys mimax, again based on comparative data from Octodontomys gliroides, is estimated to occur at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively prolonged juvenile period is several months longer than in many similarly-sized murid rodents and reflects the species' delayed reproductive maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity marks the beginning of a female's potential contribution to population growth, a process that is further constrained by the species' solitary social structure and the availability of suitable rocky outcrop territories. This life-history delay may be an adaptation to the unpredictability of high-altitude food resources, ensuring that only individuals in adequate body condition initiate breeding. Testicular development and the first scrotal descent in males likely coincide with this same age.

Basal metabolic rate, measured as the maximum oxygen consumption during rest at the species' preferred body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is estimated at 115 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 115 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This rate of oxygen consumption is comparatively low for an octodontid of its size, potentially reflecting an adaptive reduction in energy expenditure in response to the sparse, xeric vegetation of its Andean habitat. The maximum lifespan in captivity of approximately six years [am = approximately six years] is consistent with the view of this species as a slow-living, K-selected strategist at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Comparative physiological studies have shown that such a reduced metabolic rate is often coupled with enhanced longevity in small mammals, a pattern that appears to hold for Octomys mimax when considering the entire suite of its life-history traits.
